headline: Cockenoe on the Ebb, Bunker Tightening at Norwalk: The First Real Bass Are Showing
subhead: The full moon tightened bait schools like we said it would — now it's a question of which reef gets first crack at the blitz.
body_markdown:
If there's only one tide worth burning gas on this week, it's the last two hours of the ebb off Cockenoe Reef, and here's the read behind that call. Bunker schools have been tightening up hard around the Norwalk Islands over the last ten days, pushed into tighter, nervous balls by the building moon, and that kind of bait behavior is exactly what gets bigger bass to commit instead of just picking at stragglers. Cockenoe sits in the right spot to intercept that bait as it gets squeezed off the flats and funneled past the reef structure on the outgoing water — 8 to 14 feet over rock and mussel bed, current stacking bait against the drop on the northeast corner. That's where the strategy starts this week.

We flagged this a couple weeks back — said the moon building toward full on September 6-7 would tighten these bunker schools further and that the first legitimate fall blitz activity was likely within the week. The bait's doing exactly that right now, and the pieces are in place. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, still warm enough to keep the bunker comfortable and moving in tight, defensive schools rather than scattering, while water out toward New London has already dropped into the high 60s. That west-to-east gradient means Western Sound structure — Norwalk Islands, Cockenoe, Sheffield Island — is holding the most bait and the most predator interest right now. The new moon lands September 10, and that's the pivot point. Tidal flow strengthens, bait gets squeezed tighter, and if the pattern holds the way it usually does this time of year, the first real blitz behavior of the fall should show up on the back side of that moon — meaning the back half of this week into the weekend is worth having a rod rigged and ready.

Right now the bite is real but not blitz-grade yet, and it's honest to say so. Boats working bunker schools off Sheffield Island and the western edge of the Norwalk Islands are picking up striped bass in the mid-20s to high-20-inch class on bunker spoons and 2-ounce bucktails worked through the edges of the pods, plus the occasional better fish holding deeper under the school on a fresh chunk bait fished on the bottom. Bluefish are the more consistent player at the moment — choppers in the 3 to 6 pound range are tearing into the same bunker schools and will hit anything that moves fast through the surface, so a wire leader ahead of a Hopkins or a Kastmaster off the stern is producing steady action even when the bass are being coy.

Penfield Reef is fishing more like a mid-tide spot right now than a dawn-and-dusk reef. The last hour of the incoming through the first hour of the outgoing is stacking porgies thick over the rock piles in 15 to 20 feet — small green crab and sandworm on a hi-lo rig is filling coolers with fish in the 10-to-12-inch range, plenty of keepers mixed in. Blackfish are starting to show interest as water cools, though it's early — a few 3 and 4 pound tautog have come off the deeper boulder fields on the reef's south side on green crab, fished tight to structure on slack tide before the current picks up and makes bottom contact a fight.

The Cows off Stamford remain the go-to for a mixed bag when the wind kicks up and the open water gets uncomfortable — that structure breaks the current enough to fish comfortably on days the Norwalk Islands are getting hammered by weekend boat traffic and chop. Sea bass are holding steady there in 25 to 30 feet on the deeper humps, taking Gulp on light jigs, and porgies are backing them up in the same water. It's not exciting fishing, but it's dependable, and dependable matters when the bigger pattern hasn't fully turned on yet.

Fluke have faded hard from where they were in July and August, which tracks with the calendar — the bite that's left is concentrated in the deeper channel edges near Greenwich Point on the last of the outgoing, working bucktail and Gulp combinations slow along the bottom. Worth a stop if you're passing through, not worth planning a day around anymore.

As for boat traffic, Labor Day weekend cleared out and the weekday water is fishable again without dodging wakes on every drift, which matters at Cockenoe and the Norwalk Islands where the channels get tight. Early morning and late afternoon remain the clean windows on weekends still ahead.

The next few days are about watching the bunker. If those schools keep tightening the way they have been and the new moon tide on the 10th does what building tides usually do this time of year, expect the first real blitz window to open somewhere between Cockenoe and Sheffield Island — bass coming up under working bluefish and gulls, bunker getting pushed to the surface. That's the scenario worth planning around. If the bait scatters instead of tightens, fall back to the reliable reef pattern — porgies at Penfield on the tide change, sea bass at the Cows when it blows, and bluefish wherever the bunker are showing on the surface. Either way, this is the window where the season starts to turn, and the smart play is having gear rigged for both a blitz and a grind.
